statement: About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.
heath_proof: Let ABC be the given triangle; thus it is required to circumscribe a circle about the given triangle ABC. Let the straight lines AB, AC be bisected at the points D, E [I. 10], and from the points D, E let DF, EF be drawn at right angles to AB, AC; they will then meet within the triangle ABC, or on the straight line BC, or outside BC. First let them meet within at F, and let FB, FC, FA be joined. Then, since AD is equal to DB, and DF is common and at right angles, therefore the base AF is equal to the base FB. [I. 4] Similarly we can prove that CF is also equal to AF; so that FB is also equal to FC; therefore the three straight lines FA, FB, FC are equal to one another. Therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FA, FB, FC will pass also through the remaining points, and the circle will have been circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Let it be circumscribed, as ABC. Next, let DF, EF meet on the straight line BC at F, as is the case in the second figure; and let AF be joined. Then, similarly, we shall prove that the point F is the centre of the circle circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Again, let DF, EF meet outside the triangle ABC at F, as is the case in the third figure, and let AF, BF, CF be joined. Then again, since AD is equal to DB, and DF is common and at right angles, therefore the base AF is equal to the base BF. [I. 4] Similarly we can prove that CF is also equal to AF; so that BF is also equal to FC; therefore the circle described with centre F and distance one of the straight lines FA, FB, FC will pass also through the remaining points, and will have been circumscribed about the triangle ABC. Therefore about the given triangle a circle has been circumscribed.

**Statement:** About a given triangle to circumscribe a circle.

**Step 1.** Let ABC be the given triangle. It is required to circumscribe a circle about triangle ABC, that is, to describe a circle passing through the vertices A, B, and C [D4.6].

**Step 2.** Bisect the straight lines AB and AC at the points D and E respectively [1.10].

**Step 3.** From point D, draw DF at right angles to AB, and from point E, draw EF at right angles to AC [1.11].

**Step 4.** The lines DF and EF will meet either inside triangle ABC, on the side BC, or outside triangle ABC. First, let them meet inside the triangle at point F, and join FB, FA, and FC [P1].

**Step 5.** Since AD equals DB (because D is the midpoint of AB) [Step 2], and DF is common to triangles ADF and BDF, the two sides AD, DF are equal to the two sides BD, DF respectively. And angle ADF equals angle BDF, for each is a right angle [Step 3, D1.10]. Therefore, by the side-angle-side criterion, triangle ADF is congruent to triangle BDF, and hence the base FA equals the base FB [1.4].

**Step 6.** Similarly, since AE equals EC (because E is the midpoint of AC) [Step 2], and EF is common to triangles AEF and CEF, the two sides AE, EF are equal to the two sides CE, EF respectively. And angle AEF equals angle CEF, for each is a right angle [Step 3, D1.10]. Therefore triangle AEF is congruent to triangle CEF, and hence the base FA equals the base FC [1.4].

**Step 7.** Since FA equals FB [Step 5] and FA equals FC [Step 6], therefore FB equals FC [CN1]. Thus the three straight lines FA, FB, and FC are equal to one another.

**Step 8.** Therefore the circle described with centre F and radius equal to any one of FA, FB, FC will pass through the remaining vertices as well [D1.15, P3]. Let it be described and let it be the circle ABC. The circle has been circumscribed about the given triangle [D4.6].

**Step 9.** Now suppose the perpendiculars DF and EF meet on the side BC itself, say at the point F which lies on BC. Join FA [P1]. Then by the same reasoning as in Steps 5 and 6, FA equals FB and FA equals FC [1.4], so again FB equals FC [CN1]. The circle described with centre F and radius FA passes through all three vertices [D1.15, P3, D4.6].

**Step 10.** Finally, suppose the perpendiculars DF and EF meet outside triangle ABC at the point F. Join FA, FB, and FC [P1]. Again, since AD equals DB and DF is common, with angle ADF and angle BDF each being right angles, triangle ADF is congruent to triangle BDF, so FA equals FB [1.4]. Similarly, since AE equals EC and EF is common, with angle AEF and angle CEF each being right angles, triangle AEF is congruent to triangle CEF, so FA equals FC [1.4]. Therefore FB equals FC [CN1], and the circle with centre F and radius FA passes through all three vertices [D1.15, P3, D4.6].

**Step 11.** Therefore, in every case, a circle has been circumscribed about the given triangle ABC. Q.E.F.
